items.why: The final sentence explicitly contrasts the five men entering with the priest and soldiers remaining at the gate.
The sequence clearly distinguishes the five men’s initial taking from the priest’s later taking.
The trees directly ask the thornbush to be their king; gods and humans only occur in the vine’s reply.
The passage directly links their prosperity to the land lacking nothing.
A direct because-clause gives the missing inheritance as the reason, not Israel’s lack of a king.
The passage explicitly says Jotham lived there because he feared his brother Abimelek.
Abimelek addresses his mother’s brothers and clan and tells them to ask Shechem’s citizens.
The Levite’s stated purpose is finding another place to stay; Micah’s house is where he happens to arrive.
The blessing about mutual joy immediately precedes the fire statement, though calling it a request is slightly awkward.
The pronoun refers clearly to the Levite, but the phrase “does something” is notably vague.
The reported news is that Shechem’s people went into the fields; seeing them leave the city happens later.
The question carefully asks what the mother says, which names her son despite the silversmith’s later action.
The servant runs Abimelek through, and the next clause explicitly confirms Abimelek’s death.
The occupants die after branches piled against the stronghold are set on fire.
Jonathan and his sons are explicitly said to serve until the captivity, while the Shiloh period describes idol use.
The text directly places the Danites’ turning in response to the men shouting, though the pursuit also precedes it.
The fig tree’s rhetorical reply identifies giving up its sweet fruit as the reason for refusing.
The purpose clause explicitly says Abimelek approached the entrance to set the tower on fire.
The singular object of “take it over” is the land, while the people are the intended attack target.
Micah directly states that he expects favor because the Levite has become his priest.
The route supports the hill country answer, but the question’s repeated wording about the residence is cumbersome.
The immediate reference is Jerub-Baal, reinforced by Jotham’s next description of his father.
Zebul is explicitly identified as secretly sending the messengers after becoming angry at Gaal.
They address the priest and ask him to inquire of God, cleanly separating intermediary from source.
The curse is stated after the punishment, but it may describe that punishment rather than a separate later event.
Zebul directly counters Gaal’s first claim by identifying the supposed people as mountain shadows.
Jotham’s explicit purpose clause says they should listen so that God may listen to them.
The olive tree’s rhetorical answer directly cites giving up its honoring oil as the reason.
Micah tells his mother that he heard her utter the curse.
The cursing occurs while the people are eating and drinking, after the grape work is finished.
The passage explicitly attributes the lack of rescue to Laish’s distance from Sidon and absence of outside ties.
